desc:
In a binary grid, a 1 is land and a 0 is water. Two land cells are linked when they touch in any of the eight directions: horizontally, vertically or diagonally. An island is a maximal group of land cells connected through links.

Return the number of islands.

grid = [[1,0,0,1],
        [0,1,0,0],
        [0,0,0,1],
        [1,0,1,0]]   -> 4

The cells (0,0) and (1,1) form one island, (2,3) and (3,2) form another, and (0,3) and (3,0) are single-cell islands, so there are 4 islands in total.
hints: This is the classic island count, only the neighbourhood is larger.
Replace the list of four direction offsets by a list of eight: the four straight ones plus (1,1), (1,-1), (-1,1), (-1,-1).
Scan the grid; each time you meet an unvisited land cell, add one to the answer and flood-fill everything linked to it with an explicit stack.
editorial: Do the usual flood-fill island count with eight neighbour offsets instead of four. Every time the scan meets an unvisited land cell, a new island has been found: increase the counter and flood all cells linked to it, marking them visited.
Each cell is pushed at most once and looks at 8 neighbours, so the time is O(R · C) and the extra space is O(R · C) for the visited marks and the stack.
